intro: Lisbon officially records almost every notable tree in the city. Since a 2012 law, the state can formally classify select specimens as trees of public interest, and Lisbon holds more of them than any other Portuguese municipality. Its oldest are four hollow olive trees outside a hilltop chapel in Alcântara, older than the Braganza dynasty. Its strangest is a rubber fig that escaped a cracked flowerpot in Mouraria and swallowed a street. Between them sit a bleeding dragon tree, a cypress mistaken for a cedar, and the Portuguese parliament's private tipu. All but one are free to visit.
meta_description: Lisbon's oldest trees are classified by law. Meet the 457-year-old olives of Santo Amaro, a dragon tree nobody can age, and twenty more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Lisbon is one of four olive trees outside the Capela de Santo Amaro in Alcântara, estimated at around 457 years old, the only trees in the city with documented ages predating the 18th century. They stand in a small hilltop garden with a well known river view, an eleven minute walk from Alcântara-Terra train station.
question_meta: The 457-year-old olive trees of Santo Amaro are Lisbon's oldest. Their exact location, how to reach them, and twenty more remarkable trees.
question_context: Lisbon keeps its oldest trees close to its water. The four olive trees at the Capela de Santo Amaro have grown against the wall of a small circular hilltop chapel in Alcântara since sometime in the 1500s, making them roughly 457 years old by the city's own classification records, decades older than anything else on this list. The chapel itself, built in 1549, is a national monument, but the trees have outlasted several rounds of restoration to the building beside them. Their runner up in age is Lisbon's dragon tree in the Jardim Botânico da Ajuda, which was already a mature adult when transplanted into the city's first botanical garden in 1768, making it at least 258 years old. Between them, the two trees frame two very different kinds of longevity: quiet olives outside a functioning chapel, and a dramatic, half collapsed dragon tree behind paid admission and a steel prop. Getting to the olive trees is straightforward: Alcântara-Terra train station on the Cascais line, then an eleven minute walk uphill past the Miradouro de Santo Amaro, one of the better river views in the city and usually far quieter than the famous ones downtown.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lisbon?
faq.a: One of four olive trees outside the Capela de Santo Amaro in Alcântara, estimated at around 457 years old, decades older than anything else on this list.

faq.q: Are Lisbon's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: Twenty of the twenty-one are free, standing in public gardens, squares and street corners. The exception is the dragon tree at the Jardim Botanico da Ajuda, which requires a botanical garden ticket, about 1 euro, free on Sunday mornings.

faq.q: Why does Lisbon have so many classified 'trees of public interest'?
faq.a: Since a 2012 law, Portugal lets the state formally protect individual trees for their age, rarity or history. Lisbon has more classified trees than any other Portuguese municipality, concentrated mostly in its older central parishes.

Dracaena draco is a slow growing, long lived species from Macaronesia whose red sap, once called dragon's blood, was traded across medieval Europe as dye and varnish. Lisbon's specimen, in the Jardim Botânico da Ajuda, is the oldest of its kind in mainland Portugal.

trees.name: The Olive Trees of Santo Amaro

location.address: Capela de Santo Amaro, Rua de Santo Amaro, Alcântara, 1300 Lisboa

trees.story: Four olive trees outside a small round chapel in Alcântara have outlived every Portuguese king since before the Braganza dynasty existed. By the city's own classification records they are about 457 years old, the oldest documented trees in Lisbon, planted well before the Capela de Santo Amaro beside them took its current circular form in 1549. The chapel has been rebuilt and restored more than once since; the olives outside it have simply kept growing. None of the four is tall, barely six metres at most, but their trunks have hollowed and twisted with age into shapes closer to driftwood than farmland olive stock. City foresters classified them for their cultural, pedagogical and landscape interest, bureaucratic language for what amounts to old age handled well. Olive trees usually mark farmland, not clifftop chapels with river views, and these four have quietly ignored the fact that a working port and, eventually, a 25 de Abril Bridge grew up around them. The hilltop they share is one of the better free viewpoints over the Tagus, and on a typical afternoon the view gets most of the attention, while four of the oldest living things in the city stand a few steps away, propped, gnarled, and largely unbothered.
trees.access: Free, open access, public garden around the chapel
trees.transport: 11 min walk from Alcântara-Terra station (Linha de Cascais), or tram 15E to Calvário then 9 min walk

trees.name: The Ajuda Dragon Tree

location.address: Jardim Botânico da Ajuda, Calçada da Ajuda, 1300-011 Lisboa

trees.story: Cut into its bark and this tree bleeds red. The resin of Dracaena draco oxidizes into a dark crimson sap once prized across Europe as dragon's blood, used in medieval varnish, dye and folk medicine. This specimen was already a mature adult when the Italian botanist Domingos Vandelli transplanted it into Lisbon's first botanical garden in 1768, which makes it at least 258 years old and possibly closer to 400, since dragon trees carry no annual rings and nobody recorded its birth. Its crown once spread nearly 23 metres across, among the largest of its kind in the country, until a rot infection took hold around 2006 and cost it roughly half its size. A steel frame now holds up what remains. The garden, built on the grounds of the royal Ajuda Palace for King José I, treats the tree as its emblem, and cuttings from its offshoots have been propagated into a small nursery of younger dragon trees nearby. Dragon trees grow slowly and can live for centuries once established, so this one, missing half its canopy and still standing, may yet be young for its kind.
trees.access: Paid entry to Jardim Botânico da Ajuda (about 1 euro; free Sunday mornings 10:00-13:00)
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Belém station (Linha de Cascais); tram 18E stops nearby
trees.notes: Age is genuinely uncertain: the tree was already an adult specimen when transplanted in 1768 (258 years by that count alone), but several popular sources round up to 400 years assuming an earlier, undocumented origin. Presented here as a range rather than a single figure.

trees.name: The Cypress of Príncipe Real

location.address: Jardim do Príncipe Real, Praça do Príncipe Real, 1250-184 Lisboa

trees.story: Lisbon's first legally protected tree is not a cedar at all. Everyone calls it the cedro-do-Buçaco, but the tree presiding over Príncipe Real garden is Cupressus lusitanica, a cypress from the mountains of Mexico and Guatemala with a Portuguese name it never earned. In 1940 it became the first tree in the country classified as being of public interest, decades before Portugal had a formal national registry for such things. Its canopy, once a vast gazebo-like dome some 30 metres across, has thinned with age and storms down to about seven metres of visible height, though the trunk still measures four metres around at the base. Portuguese heritage records put it at roughly 150 years old, predating most of the surrounding 19th century garden. One international tree registry claims it instead dates to around 1740, nearly twice that age, a gap nobody has resolved. Locals shelter under its remaining canopy on Saturday organic market mornings, largely unaware they are standing under a tree whose paperwork outranks almost every building in view, and whose exact age is still an open question among the people paid to know it.
trees.transport: Short walk from Rato station (Metro Yellow Line)
trees.notes: Portuguese press and heritage sources converge on approximately 150 years, tied to its 1940 classification. monumentaltrees.com states it was planted around 1740, implying roughly 285 years. The discrepancy is unresolved; the more heavily corroborated 150 year figure is used as the primary estimate, per monumentaltrees being used for verification only.

trees.name: The Ombú of Largo do Limoeiro

location.address: Largo do Limoeiro, 1100-566 Lisboa

trees.story: The square is named after a lemon tree that is long gone. What replaced it as the local landmark is an ombú, a South American species with a swollen, fluted trunk that can measure some seventeen metres around at the base, wider than most house facades on the street. It grows against the outer wall of the old Limoeiro prison, a building that held political prisoners for much of the 20th century and now trains judges. Municipal archive photographs show it already a substantial adult tree by 1910, which would put its real age closer to 115 years than the 100 usually quoted. Ombú wood is famously soft and fire resistant, of no real use to carpenters, which may be exactly why this one survived when more useful trees nearby did not. It stands a few steps from the Portas do Sol viewpoint, one of the finest views over the Alfama rooftops to the river, though most visitors walk straight past its swollen trunk toward the railing. True to its local nickname, bela-sombra, beautiful shade, it still throws excellent cover over an otherwise unremarkable stretch of pavement.
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Portas do Sol tram stop (12E/28E)
trees.notes: Most sources cite 100 years; a local history blog notes the tree already appears as a mature adult in Lisbon Municipal Archive photographs from 1910, which would put its real age closer to 115 years.

trees.name: The Tipu of Jardim de São Bento

location.address: Jardim de São Bento (Praça da Constituição de 1976), Rua de São Bento, 1250-093 Lisboa

trees.story: Portugal's parliament keeps a South American tree on its doorstep. This tipu, planted around ninety years ago in the small triangular garden beside the Palácio de São Bento, blooms with orange flowers marked by a brownish red spot at the base of each petal, a native of Bolivia and Argentina with no historical connection to the 16th century Benedictine monastery the palace used to be. The monastery became the seat of the Portuguese parliament in 1834 after the religious orders were dissolved, and the garden beside it has since watched ministers, protesters and the occasional political crisis unfold a few dozen metres from its canopy. The tree is one of Lisbon's officially classified trees of public interest, a status shared by barely two dozen specimens across the entire city. Its timber, tipa, is prized in South America for furniture, though nobody here has any plans to cut this one down for a table. Late winter and spring bring its flowering season, when the garden's modest third of a hectare turns a startling shade of orange directly across the street from where the country's laws get written.
verified_sources: Portugal ICNF national register of classified trees, processo KNJ1/347, 'tipuana', Praca de S.Bento, girth 4.2m, age_register 96 (measured 2016)
trees.access: Free, public garden beside the Assembleia da República
trees.transport: 2 min walk from São Bento train station (Linha de Sintra)

best_time.label: late winter into spring, when the garden turns a startling shade of orange

trees.notes: Photo removed 2026-08-02: the approved file (Chaimite no Jardim da Praca da Constituicao de 1976) is a photograph of an armoured car parked in the garden, not of the tipu tree. Caught by Hidde on the live site. Any replacement must show the tree itself, per the Cadiz standard. Pin corrected 2026-08-06: the stored coordinate was an address-level geocode of the garden, 244m from ICNF's own surveyed point for the same species, age and classification at Praca de S.Bento (processo KNJ1/347); no second Tipuana tipu found anywhere else in the register near Sao Bento, so treated as the same tree and the register's coordinate adopted, upgrading the pin from approximate to confirmed. Found while verifying an unrelated Lisbon cluster; flagged for a session decision rather than acted on blind, then adopted because the register point is the only tree-level GPS either source has ever given this entry.

trees.name: The Coral Trees of Jardim da Luz

location.address: Jardim Teixeira Rebelo (Jardim da Luz), Largo da Luz, 1600 Lisboa

trees.story: Despite the name, this tree has never been near India. Portuguese sailors called the genus Erythrina a coral tree of the Indies after landing in Brazil convinced they had reached Asia, a five century old geography mistake baked permanently into the common name. Two specimens grow on the south side of Jardim da Luz in Carnide, both classified as trees of public interest since 1996 and both about a century old, standing twelve and fifteen metres tall. Each June they erupt in bright red flowers shaped unmistakably like a rooster's crest, the detail behind the species name crista-galli. The garden's formal name, Jardim Teixeira Rebelo, honours the founding director of the nearby Military College, though most locals still call it simply Jardim da Luz after the Baroque church across the square. A metro station sits so close to the garden gate that riders on the Blue Line surface almost directly beneath the coral trees' canopy without noticing. For two South American transplants misnamed after the wrong continent, they have settled into suburban Lisbon without complaint, flowering every summer regardless of what anyone calls them.
trees.transport: 1 min walk from Colégio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)
trees.notes: A candidate photo was checked and rejected: it is a general photo of the garden/square with no confirmation the named tree itself is in frame.

best_time.label: June, when both trees erupt in flowers shaped like a rooster's crest

trees.name: The Nettle Tree of Avenida de Berlim

location.address: Avenida de Berlim, at the junction with Avenida Francisco Luís Gomes, 1800 Lisboa

trees.story: One tree remembers the farms that used to be here. Before Lisbon's eastward expansion in the 1940s and 1950s paved over the quintas of Olivais with apartment blocks, this stretch of land was countryside, and a single European nettle tree from that era survived the building work, still standing at what is now the junction of Avenida de Berlim and Avenida Francisco Luís Gomes. Portugal's national registry of public-interest trees measured it in 2015 at 75 years old and 15.7 metres tall, younger than the round century once claimed for it but still older than the apartment blocks around it, with a broad symmetrical canopy that looks deliberately planted rather than accidentally spared, though it was almost certainly the latter. The species produces small sweet fruit that gives it a folk nickname referencing the birds that come to eat it, and its wood was historically valued for tool handles and whip stocks for its flexibility. Officially classified as a tree of public interest under process KNJ1/405, it now stands beside a bronze sculpture called Homem Sucata, Scrap Man, welded from actual car parts in 1993, an odd pairing of the area's rural past and its industrial present sharing the same traffic island. Commuters on the surrounding avenues have an older neighbour than the surrounding tower blocks suggest.
trees.transport: Roughly 15 min walk from Bela Vista station (Metro Red Line), or bus to Avenida de Berlim
trees.notes: Pin and age corrected 2026-07-26: matched to Portugal's national registry of classified trees of public interest (ICNF, si.icnf.pt/sigservices.icnf.pt), feature id 283, processo KNJ1/405, a lodao-bastardo (Celtis australis) named at exactly this junction ("Av. Berlim (cruzamento com Av Dr. Francisco Luis Gomes)"), height 15.7m matching this story's "sixteen metres" closely, last measured 2015 at age 75 (roughly 86 today). The stored pin was about 900m off (a geocode of the general avenue, not the junction); the registry point is now used instead. The registry's age (75 in 2015) conflicts with the two original tourism-site sources' "100 years" claim; treated the government measurement as authoritative and corrected the story and age fields rather than flag the conflict, since one source is a direct physical survey and the others are undated blog estimates.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Praça Paiva Couceiro

best_time.label: November, when its leaves turn uniform bright yellow and drop almost simultaneously

location.address: Praça Paiva Couceiro, 1170-284 Lisboa

trees.story: Ginkgo biloba is often called a living fossil, a species virtually unchanged for over 200 million years and one of the very few plants known to have resprouted near ground zero at Hiroshima, a resilience the species carries in its reputation rather than this particular tree's own biography. Lisbon's specimen in Praça Paiva Couceiro, in the working class Penha de França neighbourhood, is a comparatively young member of an ancient lineage: over a century old and classified as a tree of public interest, though nobody has pinned down its exact planting date. Its fan shaped leaves turn a uniform bright yellow every November before dropping almost simultaneously, a spectacle unrelated to anything else on this list and one that draws a small annual crowd of photographers to an otherwise unremarkable square. Ginkgos are dioecious, male or female, and only female trees produce the notoriously foul smelling fruit; whether this one has simply spared the neighbourhood that autumn hazard, or its sex was never recorded, nobody seems to know. Either way, it is Penha de França's one living link to a genus older than most of the world's mountain ranges.
trees.transport: Roughly 10 min walk from Arroios station (Metro Red Line)
trees.notes: No source gives a precise planting date; 'over a century old' is the most specific figure available from the two independent write-ups found so far. An earlier candidate photo was checked and rejected: it was a general shot of the square with no confirmation the tree itself was in frame. A second candidate, File:Plantano na Praça Paiva Couceiro, Lisboa, 2024.jpg, was added at found_needs_check on 2026-07-29 on the strength of a paraphrased caption; that paraphrase was wrong. 2026-07-29 (later session): downloaded and personally viewed the file plus re-checked its Commons metadata directly via the API. Both the file's own title/description ('Plantano na Praça Paiva Couceiro', Portuguese for plane tree) and the photo itself (lobed plane-tree leaves, not ginkgo's fan shape) show a Platanus, not this tree's Ginkgo biloba. Reverted to missing. Also searched the Praça Paiva Couceiro Commons category (3 files, none a ginkgo) and several ginkgo/nogueira-do-japão query variants: no genuine match exists yet. Real dead end, not a tooling gap.

trees.name: The Paineira of Jardim Alfredo Keil

location.address: Jardim Alfredo Keil, Praça da Alegria, 1250-004 Lisboa
location.neighbourhood: Praça da Alegria, Avenida da Liberdade

trees.story: Every October this tree turns a small garden pink. The silk floss tree in Jardim Alfredo Keil is one of six individually classified specimens within a nine tree ensemble that the city declared collectively of public interest in 2017, a South American species whose thorny green trunk and cotton candy coloured blooms have become an unofficial marker of autumn across Lisbon in recent years. The garden itself, laid out in 1882 on the former site of the Feira da Ladra flea market before that market moved to Alfama, is barely large enough to contain the tree's crown, and a bust of the composer Alfredo Keil, who wrote the melody that became Portugal's national anthem, watches from one corner. No source isolates exactly how old this particular paineira is, since the 2017 classification covers the whole collection of trees rather than dating each specimen individually. The fruit that follows the flowers splits open to release seeds wrapped in a silky white floss, once used to stuff pillows and life jackets, a soft, practical footnote to a tree that spends every autumn putting on the loudest show in the neighbourhood.
trees.transport: 6 min walk from Restauradores station (Metro Blue Line)
trees.notes: This paineira is one of six individually classified trees within a nine-tree ensemble at Jardim Alfredo Keil, classified collectively in 2017. No source isolates this specimen's individual age. Photo is iNaturalist observation 249878863 (2024-10-31), a Ceiba speciosa in bloom 28m from this pin, well within the small garden. Viewed directly 2026-07-26: shows a mature trunk and branches covered in the characteristic pink, white-throated blooms of Ceiba speciosa against an urban backdrop consistent with Praça da Alegria, matching both the species and the location closely enough to approve despite the observer's ID being casual-grade rather than community-confirmed. Pin confirmed 2026-07-26 against Portugal's national registry of classified trees (ICNF), feature id 316, a conjunto arboreo (tree grouping) at Praca da Alegria listing exactly the garden's known species mix (2 Ceiba speciosa/crispiflora, 2 Metrosideros excelsa, 2 Erythrina crista-galli, 1 Celtis australis, 1 Washingtonia robusta), protected since 1970 with the 2017 classification adding to it. The registry's own point (38.717875, -9.145227) sits within 2m of the stored pin, so treated as confirmed even though, like the story itself says, the classification covers the ensemble rather than isolating this one paineira from its five neighbours.

best_time.label: October, when the tree turns the garden pink

trees.name: The Giant Rubber Tree of Mouraria
trees.label: Urban curiosity

location.address: Rua de São Cristóvão 22-24, Mouraria, 1100-177 Lisboa

trees.story: Nobody knows how this tree got here, and that is most of its appeal. A rubber fig now towers some six metres over a narrow street in Mouraria, its roots having escaped a cracked pot years ago and driven straight into the ground below, its trunk and branches now filling the gap between two building facades on Rua de São Cristóvão as though it had been planted there on purpose. It was not. Plant researchers who have examined it, including the botanist André Mota, can confirm the species and describe its improvised growth, but not its origin story. Unlike the classified trees of public interest elsewhere on this list, this one carries no official age, no protected status and no municipal plaque, just several hundred enthusiastic online reviews and a café that opened next door in 2022 partly because of the foot traffic the tree now draws. It is the youngest and least official entry here, almost certainly under 40 years old, included not for its age but for the fact that a potted houseplant broke loose and quietly became one of the most photographed trees in the neighbourhood.
trees.transport: Short walk from Martim Moniz station (Metro Green Line)
trees.notes: Not an ancient tree: origin and exact age are unknown, and researchers who have examined it consider it a modern escapee from a broken pot, likely under 40 years old. Included for its visual spectacle and local renown rather than its age, per the qualifying criteria in CLAUDE.md. No official classification or protected status; access and public visibility are well documented, unlike its history.

trees.name: The Fig of the Estrela Garden

location.address: Jardim da Estrela (Jardim Guerra Junqueiro), Praça da Estrela, 1200-667 Lisboa

trees.story: Lisbon has bolted a metal plate to this trunk, and where the age should be it says one word: unknown. That is unusually honest for a municipality, and it is also the most interesting thing about the tree. The garden around it opened in April 1852 after ten years of stop-start construction, so the fig cannot be much more than a century and three quarters old, which for something this bulky is the surprise. Moreton Bay figs grow at a speed that makes ordinary trees look idle. The plate arrived in 2020, when Lisbon gave 27,610 of its trees an identity card and hung QR codes on around 750 of them. Look up and you see why this species unsettles people: aerial roots hang from the limbs like rope, and where they reach soil they thicken into new trunks, so the tree slowly becomes a colony of itself. It is not alone here either. At least five mature figs stand in these five hectares, and the one at the pond's edge, roots spilling over the kerb toward the ducks, is the one everybody photographs.
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Estrela (Basílica), then about 2 min walk
trees.notes: Age is genuinely undocumented: Lisbon's own QR identification plate on this tree records the age as 'desconhecida'. The range given is bounded by the garden's 1852 opening and calibrated against ICNF-classified Ficus macrophylla elsewhere in Lisbon (Príncipe Real 145 years, Largo Hintze Ribeiro 100, Jardim Constantino 107). Not in the ICNF register: the nearest classified tree is 494m away. Pin is the fig at the pond's edge, the photographed and most-visited of the park's five or more mature figs; approximate because the park's figs are scattered and no source distinguishes them individually.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of the Estrela Garden
trees.age_estimate: unknown, planted after the garden opened in 1852

location.address: Jardim da Estrela (Jardim Guerra Junqueiro), Praça da Estrela, 1200-667 Lisboa

trees.story: Nobody can tell you how old this tree is, and that is a property of the species rather than a gap in the paperwork. A dragon tree is not a tree in the ordinary sense: it lays down no annual rings, so the one method that reliably ages an oak or a beech simply does not apply. Botanists count branch generations instead, because the crown forks only after each flowering, which happens at intervals of a decade or more. What that produces is this shape, a trunk splitting into a tight umbrella of stiff blue-green blades that looks less grown than engineered. Cut the bark and the sap runs red, which is where the name comes from and why the resin was traded across medieval Europe as dragon's blood, used for varnish, medicine and dye. The species belongs to the Canary Islands and Madeira, where it is now scarce in the wild. This one has stood among the palms and benches near the centre of the garden since some point after 1852, quietly outliving every gardener who has worked around it, and Lisbon has a second on our map in the botanical garden at Ajuda.
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Estrela (Basílica), then about 2 min walk
trees.notes: No published age exists and dragon trees cannot be aged by rings; the range is bounded only by the garden's 1852 opening. Not in the ICNF register. Pin is a 12-observation iNaturalist centroid with under 19m spread, all with stated accuracy of 10m or better, so the individual is identifiable on the ground.

trees.name: The Strangler Fig of Príncipe Real

location.address: Jardim França Borges, Praça do Príncipe Real, 1250-096 Lisboa

trees.story: Everyone in this square looks at the cypress. It sits under a metal frame like a green table, it was the first tree in Lisbon given legal protection, in 1940, and it takes all the photographs. Three Australian figs stand around it and almost nobody registers them, which is odd, because they are the reason the square feels roofed. This one carries the thickest trunk of the three, just over six metres around, and holds its crown twenty one metres up. Ficus macrophylla does not start life as a tree in Australia. It germinates in the fork of another one, drops roots down the host's trunk and thickens them until the host is enclosed and dies, which is why the species is called a strangler. Here it had nothing to strangle, so the aerial roots simply hang, reach the gravel and stiffen into props. Underneath all of this is water. The Patriarcal reservoir was finished in 1864, an octagonal chamber on thirty one pillars holding 880 cubic metres for the city, and the garden is its lid. On Saturday mornings a producers' market sets up between the trunks.
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all times
trees.transport: Metro Rato (yellow line), about 6 min walk uphill, or tram 24E to Praça do Príncipe Real
trees.notes: ICNF processo AIP11066144I, 'figueira-da-baía-de-moreton (n.º 2)', classified D.R. n.º 11, II Série, 14/01/2004. Register figures: girth 6.05 m, height 21 m, age 145 at the 2015 survey, so about 156 in 2026. Independent second source florestas.pt, which describes three classified Australian figs in this garden of roughly the same age as the columnar araucaria, about 140 years, 'que se destacam pelas suas dimensões e raízes aéreas'. The two age figures (145 at 2015 versus about 140 at publication) do not reconcile exactly, hence the 140-160 range and the flag. Pin is approximate on purpose: the register surveys n.º 1 (AIP11066142I, girth 4.80 m) and n.º 3 (AIP11066145I, girth 4.70 m) at 49 m and 26 m from this point, all three are Ficus macrophylla in the same square, and no source on the ground tells a visitor which numbered tree is which. Stand at the largest. The other two processos are recorded as leads. Not to be confused with lis_003, the Cupressus lusitanica 24 m away in the same square.

trees.name: The Yew of Campo Santana

location.address: Jardim Braamcamp Freire, Campo dos Mártires da Pátria, 1150-230 Lisboa

trees.story: A European yew has no business growing here. The species belongs to damp northern churchyards and mountain shade, and Lisbon offers neither, yet this one has put on close to four metres of girth and fourteen metres of height on a hill above the Avenida. Portugal classified it in May 1968, which makes it one of the earliest protected trees in the city, and the national register now puts it a little past 130 years old. The ground under it has a harder history than the lawns suggest. This field held a slaughterhouse and then a bullring, and in 1817 the men condemned with Gomes Freire de Andrade were hanged on it, which is how Campo de Santana became Campo dos Mártires da Pátria. The garden came afterwards, laid out around a lake with exotic birds wandering the paths, and the medical school and the Hospital de São José still crowd its edges. At the top of the same field stands the statue of Sousa Martins, a physician who died in 1897, its plinth buried under marble plaques left by people who believe he still answers. Every part of a yew is poisonous except the red flesh around the seed.
trees.transport: Metro Intendente (green line), about 8 min walk, or Metro Avenida (blue line), about 10 min
trees.notes: ICNF processo AIP11065607I, 'teixo', classified D.G. n.º 121, II Série, 21/05/1968 and re-published D.R. n.º 115, II Série, 18/06/2018. Register figures: girth 3.80 m, height 14 m, age 123 at the 2016 survey, so about 133 in 2026. Second source: Wikipedia PT 'Jardim Braamcamp Freire' independently lists Taxus baccata L. among the garden's árvores de interesse público under the same 1968 diploma. One unresolved point recorded rather than published: a search snippet claims two classified yews here, one from 1968 and one from 2000, but the register holds only this one teixo and the Wikipedia list names only one, so the story does not claim a pair. Pin is the register's own surveyed point and this is the only classified yew in the garden, hence confirmed.

trees.name: The Weeping Fig of Campo Santana

location.address: Jardim Braamcamp Freire, Campo dos Mártires da Pátria, 1150-230 Lisboa

trees.story: Ficus benjamina is the tree most people know as a pot plant, the glossy thing sulking in an office corner and shedding leaves whenever somebody moves it. Fifty paces from the yew, on the same slope, one of them has a trunk five metres around and a crown twenty metres up. Portugal classified it on exactly the same day as the yew, 21 May 1968, and the national register still files it under a second name that says what the species does when nothing stops it: matapalo, tree killer. Like its Moreton Bay relatives it can begin high in another tree and work downward, and even planted honestly in soil it keeps the habit of letting fine roots down from the limbs. One useful correction before you go. The register maps a single specimen here. Portuguese sources describing the garden count two of them, classified together under the same 1968 diploma. That gap between a national list and what a city actually holds is completely normal, so expect a pair and stand at the bigger one. The garden around them runs to twenty eight tree species, a Himalayan cedar and a paper mulberry among them, so the fig is not the only import that outgrew its label.
trees.transport: Metro Intendente (green line), about 8 min walk, or Metro Avenida (blue line), about 10 min

(dois exemplares)' under the same 1968 diploma. trees.name: The Taxodium of the Jardim da Parada
trees.age_estimate: unknown, not recorded in the national register

location.address: Jardim Teófilo Braga (Jardim da Parada), Rua Coelho da Rocha, 1350-075 Lisboa

trees.story: Six and a half metres around the trunk and twenty six metres up, this is the largest tree in a garden that fills one whole city block, and for four years it has been at the centre of an argument about a railway. Lisbon is building a metro station under Campo de Ourique. The worksite takes a slice of the garden, residents formed a movement to stop it, and in 2024 they tied coloured ribbons through the branches: black for a tree to be felled, red for high risk of dying, yellow for at risk. The metro company's public answer was a twenty metre radius around the garden's three classified trees with no work inside it and continuing health checks, with six unclassified hackberries taken out instead, four of them replanted in the same holes. The tree carries a small taxonomic dispute of its own. The national register lists it as Taxodium mucronatum, the Montezuma cypress of Mexican riverbanks, the species that produced the widest trunk ever measured on a tree. The parish council and the Portuguese encyclopedia both call it a bald cypress. Nobody has published a resolution. The garden was the parade ground of the Campo de Ourique barracks, which is why nobody calls it by the president's name.
trees.access: Free, public garden. A metro construction site takes part of the block until at least the end of 2026 and paths move around it; the classified trees sit inside a protected radius away from the works
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Campo de Ourique, then about 5 min walk
trees.notes: ICNF processo AIP11065946I, 'taxódio ou cipreste-mexicano', classified Despacho (extrato) n.º 8497/2018, D.R. 2.ª série n.º 169, 3 September 2018. Register figures: girth 6.60 m, height 26 m, last measured 2009. SPECIES CONFLICT, unresolved and therefore flagged: ICNF records Taxodium mucronatum, while Wikipedia PT and the Junta de Freguesia de Campo de Ourique both say Taxodium distichum. The register is the classifying authority so its name is used; note that T. mucronatum is treated by some authorities as a Mexican variety of T. distichum, so the two may not be a real disagreement. AGE: the register leaves the age field empty for all three classified trees in this garden and no other source supplies one, so the 80-150 range is a wide bound from trunk size and the neighbourhood's own build-out, not a measurement. COUNT CORRECTION, worth keeping: Wikipedia PT and the parish both describe four classified trees here including a Sequoia sempervirens, but the national register holds exactly three processos, and the metro's own environmental documents refer to 'as três árvores classificadas' and '3 exemplares arbóreos classificados'. Never write four. ALIVE: photographed standing in this garden by two different Commons contributors, most recently 14 June 2024; the metro's felling list names six unclassified Celtis australis, not this tree. Photo viewed at full size before approval: the tree fills the frame in daylight, trunk and crown both readable, bandstand to the right, centre band holds the trunk so the card crop survives.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of the Jardim da Parada
trees.age_estimate: unknown, not recorded in the national register

location.address: Jardim Teófilo Braga (Jardim da Parada), Rua Coelho da Rocha, 1350-075 Lisboa

trees.story: Two of them stand ten metres apart at the edge of this garden and the register protects them as separate trees, which is fair enough: one measures 4.55 metres around the trunk, the other 4.9. From underneath they read as a single thing, a low tangle of grey limbs running almost horizontally out over the pavement with curtains of aerial root hanging off them, more like a tree that fell and carried on than one that stood up straight. Metrosideros excelsa comes from the coast of New Zealand's North Island, where it grips volcanic cliffs with exactly those roots. In Campo de Ourique it grips a kerb. Flowering lands in May and June here, half a year away from the December bloom that made it a Christmas tree at home, and it is not a subtle event: the crown fills with crimson stamens and almost no petal worth the name, and the pavement underneath goes red as they drop. Both trees were classified in September 2018, late for something this size, and both now sit inside the twenty metre no-work radius the metro company promised around the garden's classified trees.

trees.name: The Tipuana of the Ninth of April Garden

location.address: Jardim 9 de Abril, Rua das Janelas Verdes, 1200-690 Lisboa

trees.story: This garden is named after a defeat. On 9 April 1918 the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps was overrun at La Lys in Flanders in the course of one morning, and Lisbon put the date on a small terrace above the river. The tipuana shades most of it: twenty two metres tall, three and a fifth metres round the trunk, classified in 2001 along with two neighbours, and by the national register's arithmetic somewhere near 145 years old now. Tipuana tipu is Bolivian and Argentine, a legume that behaves like a plane tree in Mediterranean cities and gets planted everywhere for it, along whole Lisbon avenues. What it does that plane trees do not is drip. In warm months the canopy releases a fine sticky rain, honeydew from the sap-feeding insects living in it, and anyone who has parked a car under one does not do it twice. The ground itself was the walled garden of the Albertas, a Carmelite convent, before the city took it over. Two older names for the place survive in daily use because of that, Jardim das Albertas and Jardim da Rocha do Conde de Óbidos. Walk to the parapet and the Tagus opens up, container cranes and all.
trees.access: Free, municipal garden with permanent public access. This is not the museum's own garden next door and no ticket is needed
trees.transport: Bus 727 or 713 stops on Rua das Janelas Verdes at the Museu de Arte Antiga, 1 min walk; from Santos station it is about 8 min uphill
trees.notes: ICNF processo KNJ1/400, 'tipuana', classified Aviso n.º 15 612/2001, D.R. 2.ª série. Register figures: girth 3.20 m, height 22.2 m, age 133 at the 2015 survey, so about 144 in 2026. Second source: Portal do Jardim's page on the garden names 'Tipuana tipu, Brachychiton e Phoenix dactylifera' as the garden's árvores classificadas de interesse público, an independent confirmation of species and place. Garden verified in an earlier pass as a municipal garden with permanent public access ('jardim de acesso público permanente', Wikipedia PT), distinct from the Jardim do Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga immediately next door, which is bound to museum hours and currently under renovation. Sources conflate the two constantly; the register's lugar for all three trees is Jardim 9 de Abril. Area 3,402 m2, of which 2,373 m2 green space. Named for 9 April 1918, the Battle of La Lys. Second tipuana in the Lisbon file after lis_005, a different classified tree 1.0 km away.

trees.name: The Date Palm of the Ninth of April Garden

location.address: Jardim 9 de Abril, Rua das Janelas Verdes, 1200-690 Lisboa

trees.story: Lisbon's city hall calls this the tallest tree in the city and puts it at 38 metres, four metres over the triumphal arch at the bottom of the Baixa. The national register measured it in 2015 and wrote down 26.7. Both figures are published, neither has been reconciled, and standing at the foot of it you will not settle the question either, because a date palm gives the eye nothing to measure against: no branches, no taper, just a grey column of old leaf bases and then a burst of fronds a long way up. Phoenix dactylifera is a desert crop from Mesopotamia and North Africa, grown for its fruit for at least five thousand years and almost never allowed to get this tall, because an orchard keeps its palms low enough to climb and harvest. Nobody was harvesting this one. It was classified in 2001 along with the tipuana and the flame tree beside it, and the register's clock puts it near 145 years. The trunk is barely one and a half metres around. It has held all that up for a century and a half, on the lip of a terrace above the Tagus that flatters the height even further.
trees.access: Free, municipal garden with permanent public access. This is not the museum's own garden next door and no ticket is needed
trees.transport: Bus 727 or 713 stops on Rua das Janelas Verdes at the Museu de Arte Antiga, 1 min walk; from Santos station it is about 8 min uphill
trees.notes: ICNF processo KNJ1/402, 'tamareira', classified Aviso n.º 15 612/2001, D.R. 2.ª série. Register figures: girth 1.62 m, height 26.7 m, age 133 at the 2015 survey, so about 144 in 2026. Second source: Correio da Manhã's data feature on Lisbon's trees, which cites the Câmara Municipal de Lisboa calling this the tallest tree in the city at 38 m, taller than the 34 m Arco da Rua Augusta; Portal do Jardim independently confirms Phoenix dactylifera as one of the garden's three classified trees. HEIGHT CONFLICT, flagged and stated in the story rather than resolved: 38 m (municipality) versus 26.7 m (national register, 2015). Both are published claims, no source reconciles them, and the entry does not pick a winner. The 'tallest tree in Lisbon' claim is presented as the municipality's, not as our own, per hard rule 8. Neither claim is repeated as a superlative anywhere else in the corpus.

trees.name: The Tipuana of Jardim Roque Gameiro

location.address: Jardim Roque Gameiro (Jardim do Cais do Sodré), Cais do Sodré, Lisboa

verified_sources: data/registers/portugal-icnf.json (processo KNJ1/403, D.R. n.º 298, II Série de 27/12/2001, girth 2.98m, age_register 105 at last_measured 2015)
trees.access: Free, public garden beside Cais do Sodré station
trees.transport: Cais do Sodré station (Metro Green Line, train and ferry hub), 2 minute walk, the garden is directly adjacent
trees.story: This tree stands in the middle of a bus terminal, and that is the honest story rather than something to smooth over. The garden, popularly called Jardim do Cais do Sodre, sits exactly where the Sintra and Cascais railway lines, the Green Line metro and the Cacilhas ferry all converge, one of the first patches of green a visitor arriving into Lisbon by train or boat actually walks past. For years Carris buses ate most of the available space; a renovation under the city's 'A Square in Each Neighbourhood' programme has been handing some of it back. Through all of it, a single Tipuana tipu has kept growing at the centre, classified a Tree of Public Interest since 2001 and now roughly 115 years old, a South American species that reached Lisbon long before anyone built a transit hub around it. Its trunk runs just under three metres round. Nearby stands a bronze sculpture called Homem do Leme, the Helmsman, and an old kiosk once used as a ticket office, both easier to notice than the tree that predates them. Come between February and May and the argument for stopping gets easier: the canopy turns a burnt orange with clustered flowers, briefly outshining the buses idling underneath it.

best_time.label: February to May, when the canopy turns burnt orange above the bus terminal

trees.name: The Tipuana of Praça São João Bosco

location.address: Jardim da Parada dos Prazeres, Praça São João Bosco, 1350-297 Lisboa

verified_sources: data/registers/portugal-icnf.json (processo AIP11066049I, classified Despacho (extrato) n.º 782/2019, Diário da República 2.ª série n.º 13, 18 January 2019, girth 3.42m, height 23.5m, crown 34m, age_register 100 at last_measured 2010)
trees.access: Free, public garden and traffic circle, open at all hours
trees.transport: Tram 25E to Campo de Ourique / Prazeres, then about a 5 minute walk
trees.story: A tree with a thirty four metre crown grows in the middle of a traffic circle, and by 2018 that crown had become the problem. City arborists and technicians from Portugal's nature institute came out that March to relieve the load: selective limb removal, canopy thinning, cuts meant to let wind pass through rather than push against it, the kind of surgery a tree this size needs to keep standing over a road. The garden that holds it, seven thousand square metres wrapped around a statue of Don Bosco raised in 1988, forms the roundabout that carries traffic between Campo de Ourique and the Prazeres district, directly across from Lisbon's second largest cemetery. The national register measured the tipu's trunk at 100 years old back in 2010, putting it past its first century now, a South American import from the subtropical lowlands of Bolivia and Argentina. It earned legal protection as a tree of public interest in January 2019, one of a few dozen trees in Lisbon to hold that status. Its trunk runs 3.4 metres round, modest next to the spread it throws overhead. Late spring dusts the roundabout's lawns orange when it flowers. Cars circle it a thousand times a day; almost none of the drivers know what they are driving around.
trees.notes: ICNF processo AIP11066049I, Tipuana tipu, Praça São João Bosco / Jardim da Parada dos Prazeres, classified Despacho (extrato) n.º 782/2019, Diário da República 2.ª série n.º 13, 18 January 2019. Register figures: girth 3.42 m, height 23.5 m, crown 34 m, last measured 2010 at age 100 (register-only figure; AGE FLAGGED, no independent age source found). Second source for existence, species and status: Junta de Freguesia da Estrela's own news article on a March 2018 structural pruning of this exact tree, carried out with ICNF oversight. THIS IS A DIFFERENT GARDEN from lis_016/lis_017's 'Jardim da Parada' (Jardim Teofilo Braga, the Campo de Ourique barracks parade ground, roughly 500 m north): this one is Jardim da Parada dos Prazeres, a 7,000 sqm roundabout garden around the Sao Joao Bosco statue (inaugurated 1988), facing the Prazeres Cemetery, straddling Campo de Ourique and Estrela parishes (register lists freguesia as Estrela). Confirmed as a separate location by web search before naming, given the corpus already flags this exact 'two gardens share a nickname' risk on lis_016. Distance to the nearest existing published tree (lis_017, the Pohutukawa) is about 500 m, inside the walk radius: joins the Estrela cluster (lis_005, lis_011, lis_012, lis_016, lis_017) as its sixth tree.
